creator_or_source: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
year_introduced: 2024 (published in EU Official Journal 12 July 2024, entered into force 1 August 2024, phased enforcement through 2027)
scope: Governance — Full lifecycle regulation of AI systems placed on the EU market, classifying them by risk level with corresponding obligations for providers, deployers, importers, and distributors
key_components:
The EU AI Act establishes a four-tier, risk-based classification system for AI systems operating in or affecting the EU market. Each tier carries different regulatory obligations:

**Tier 1 — Unacceptable Risk (Prohibited, Article 5):** Eight categories of AI practices are outright banned: (1) subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques distorting behaviour and causing significant harm; (2) exploiting vulnerabilities related to age, disability, or socio-economic circumstances; (3) social scoring — evaluating individuals based on social behaviour or personal traits leading to detrimental treatment; (4) assessing individual criminal risk solely based on profiling or personality traits; (5) inferring emotions in workplaces or educational institutions (except medical/safety); (6) biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes like race, political opinions, religion, or sexual orientation; (7) untargeted scraping of facial images from internet or CCTV to build facial recognition databases; (8) real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement (with narrow exceptions for missing persons, imminent threats, and serious crime suspects). Penalties: up to EUR 35M or 7% of worldwide annual turnover.

**Tier 2 — High Risk (Annex I and Annex III):** AI systems are classified high-risk if they are: (a) safety components or products covered by EU laws in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment, or (b) listed in the eight Annex III use-case areas: (1) non-banned biometrics (remote biometric identification, biometric categorisation, emotion recognition); (2) critical infrastructure safety components (digital infrastructure, road traffic, water/gas/heating/electricity supply); (3) education and vocational training (admissions, learning outcome evaluation, student monitoring); (4) employment and worker management (recruitment, CV screening, performance evaluation, task allocation, promotion/termination decisions); (5) essential public and private services (benefits eligibility, creditworthiness evaluation, emergency call classification, health/life insurance risk assessment); (6) law enforcement (crime victim risk assessment, polygraphs, evidence reliability, re-offending risk, criminal profiling); (7) migration, asylum, and border control (polygraphs, irregular migration risk, asylum/visa applications, identification of individuals); (8) administration of justice and democratic processes (legal research and fact application, influencing elections/voting behaviour). High-risk providers must implement: risk management systems, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, instructions for use, human oversight mechanisms, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity standards, and quality management systems. Penalties: up to EUR 15M or 3% of turnover.

**Tier 3 — Limited Risk (Article 50, Transparency Obligations):** AI systems interacting directly with people, generating or manipulating content (deepfakes), or classifying as emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems must meet transparency requirements: (1) inform users they are interacting with AI (chatbots); (2) disclose that content has been artificially generated or manipulated (deepfakes); (3) mark AI-generated synthetic audio, image, video, or text in machine-readable format. A Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content was drafted in December 2025.

**Tier 4 — Minimal Risk (No specific obligations):** The vast majority of AI applications (spam filters, AI-enabled video games, recommendation systems, inventory management) face no specific regulatory requirements. Voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.

**General Purpose AI (GPAI) Models — Separate Obligations:** All GPAI providers must provide technical documentation, instructions for downstream providers, respect the Copyright Directive, and publish a training data summary. GPAI models with systemic risk (compute > 10^25 FLOPs) must additionally conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, track and report serious incidents, and ensure cybersecurity. Free/open-licence GPAI models have lighter obligations unless they present systemic risk.
typical_use_case: An AI startup building a recruitment screening tool must first classify their system under the EU AI Act. Since AI for employment (CV screening, candidate evaluation) falls under Annex III Area 4 (Employment and Workers Management), it is classified as high-risk. The startup must then implement the full suite of high-risk obligations: establish a risk management system, ensure training data is representative and free of discriminatory bias, create technical documentation, build in human oversight so recruiters can override AI decisions, conduct a conformity assessment, register in the EU database, and affix the CE marking before placing the product on the EU market. In contrast, if the same startup builds a general chatbot for customer support, it only needs to ensure transparency (inform users they are talking to AI) — a limited-risk obligation.
deliverables: Risk classification determination, conformity assessment reports, technical documentation, risk management system documentation, fundamental rights impact assessment (for deployers of high-risk systems), CE marking (for high-risk systems), EU database registration, quality management system documentation, transparency disclosures
genai_relevance: High — The EU AI Act directly addresses Generative AI through its GPAI model provisions (Chapter V). All GPAI model providers (including LLM providers like OpenAI, Mistral, Anthropic) must provide technical documentation, training data summaries, and comply with the Copyright Directive. GPAI models exceeding 10^25 FLOPs in training compute are classified as presenting systemic risk with additional obligations for model evaluation and adversarial testing. Generative AI outputs (text, image, audio, video) trigger Article 50 transparency obligations requiring machine-readable labelling. The December 2025 draft Code of Practice specifically addresses AI-generated content labelling for deepfakes and synthetic media. Startups using or fine-tuning foundation models inherit provider or deployer obligations depending on how much they modify the base model.
accessibility_for_non_engineers: High — The four-tier risk pyramid (Unacceptable > High > Limited > Minimal) is intuitive and designed for non-technical stakeholders to understand. The European Commission provides a free online Compliance Checker tool at artificialintelligenceact.eu that walks users through simple questions to determine their obligations. The Small Businesses' Guide to the AI Act provides accessible explanations. However, determining the exact classification of a specific AI system and navigating the detailed compliance requirements for high-risk systems does require legal or technical expertise.
time_to_apply: Initial risk classification: 1-2 hours using the EU Compliance Checker. Full compliance for high-risk systems: multi-month ongoing process including conformity assessment, technical documentation, risk management system setup, and quality management system establishment. For limited/minimal risk: days to implement transparency notices.
free_or_paid: Free — The regulation text, compliance checker, and official guidance are freely available. The EU AI Office provides free regulatory sandbox access for SMEs. However, achieving compliance for high-risk systems typically requires legal consulting and may involve paid conformity assessment by notified bodies.
adoption_level: Industry standard — The EU AI Act is the world's first comprehensive AI regulation. It is legally binding across all 27 EU Member States and applies to any organization worldwide whose AI system's output is used in the EU. It has become the de facto global reference framework for AI regulation, with similar legislation being developed in other jurisdictions. Companies worldwide are aligning their AI governance with the EU AI Act given its extraterritorial reach.
ai_project_stage: Multiple — Applies across the entire AI system lifecycle. Classification happens at Ideation/PoC stage. Compliance requirements (risk management, data governance, documentation) must be built in from development through Production and Maintenance. Ongoing monitoring and incident reporting obligations extend through the entire operational life of the system.
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: The EU AI Act is the single most important regulatory factor for any entrepreneur building or deploying AI in the European market. It determines: (1) Whether your product is even legal to build (prohibited tier eliminates entire product categories like social scoring or manipulative AI); (2) Your compliance cost and time-to-market (high-risk systems require months of preparation vs. days for minimal risk); (3) Your competitive moat (compliance creates barriers to entry — startups that invest early gain first-mover advantage); (4) Your go-to-market strategy (risk classification dictates documentation, certification, and deployment requirements). Crucially, the Act includes SME-friendly provisions: simplified technical documentation forms, priority access to regulatory sandboxes free of charge, proportional penalties (whichever is lower, not higher), dedicated support channels, and reduced conformity assessment fees. Understanding risk classification is the first strategic decision for any AI startup targeting Europe.
session_mapping: S5 (Ethics/Governance) — Primary session for deep-dive into the Act's risk tiers, prohibited practices, and compliance obligations. Also relevant to S3 (Projects) for integrating compliance into AI project planning and S4 (Business Models) for understanding regulatory impact on market entry and unit economics.
complements: Pairs naturally with NIST AI RMF (provides the practical risk management methodology that helps fulfill the Act's risk management obligations for high-risk systems), ISO 42001 (provides the management system structure to operationalize ongoing compliance), AI Canvas and CRISP-DM (the Act's risk classification should be integrated as a gate in early project planning phases), and Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment templates (required for deployers of high-risk systems under Article 27).
limitations: The Act is still in phased implementation (full enforcement for high-risk Annex III systems not until August 2026, Annex I until August 2027), creating regulatory uncertainty. Guidelines specifying practical classification examples won't be published until February 2026. The boundary between high-risk and limited-risk can be ambiguous for novel AI applications. Compliance costs for high-risk systems may be disproportionately burdensome for early-stage startups despite SME provisions. The Act is EU-specific — entrepreneurs operating globally must also navigate other jurisdictions' AI regulations. GPAI model obligations create upstream complexity for startups using third-party foundation models. The regulation was largely designed pre-ChatGPT and the GPAI provisions were added later, leading to some conceptual tensions between the risk-based approach for specific AI systems and the horizontal obligations for general-purpose models.
example_application: A French startup, 'EduScore AI', wants to build an AI-powered platform that evaluates student exam answers and provides personalized learning recommendations for French universities. Step 1 — Risk Classification: AI for 'evaluating learning outcomes' falls under Annex III Area 3 (Education and Vocational Training), making it high-risk. Step 2 — Compliance Roadmap: The startup must implement a risk management system (identify bias risks in grading, ensure fairness across demographics), establish data governance (ensure training datasets represent diverse student populations), create technical documentation, build human oversight (professors can review and override AI grades), achieve accuracy/robustness standards, and set up a quality management system. Step 3 — Conformity Assessment: Before launch, EduScore AI must complete a conformity assessment, register in the EU database, and affix CE marking. Step 4 — Ongoing Obligations: Post-deployment monitoring, incident reporting, and periodic reviews. Estimated timeline: 4-6 months for compliance preparation before market launch. The startup leverages the EU's regulatory sandbox program for early testing and simplified documentation as an SME.

regulatory_alignment: EU AI Act (this IS the regulation), GDPR (complementary — AI systems processing personal data must comply with both; the AI Act explicitly references GDPR data protection requirements), NIST AI RMF (voluntary framework that maps well to the Act's risk management requirements), ISO 42001 (international standard that provides management system structure aligned with the Act's quality management obligations)
